source_excerpt: About 70–80% of the 250–300 mg of bilirubin produced each day is derived from the breakdown of hemoglobin in senescent red blood cells.

Not found (searched: 250, 300 mg, 70–80%, senescent, myoglobin, reticuloendothelial, spleen)
new_contribution: About 250–300 mg of bilirubin is produced daily; 70–80% comes from haemoglobin of senescent red cells, the remainder from prematurely destroyed erythroid cells in the marrow and turnover of haemoproteins such as myoglobin. Bilirubin is formed in reticuloendothelial cells, primarily in the spleen and liver.
reason: Quantitative and site detail absent from book; useful for understanding haemolytic and shunt hyperbilirubinaemia.

source_excerpt: After entering the hepatocyte, unconjugated bilirubin is bound to the cytosolic protein ligandin.
topic: Hepatic processing of bilirubin: four steps, ligandin, canalicular secretion
book_has: p245: 'Carrier mediated uptake by hepatic cells, Conjugation to glucuronic acid and Excretion into bile'; unconjugated bilirubin 'tightly complexed to serum albumin'. Not found (searched: ligandin, cytosolic binding, endoplasmic reticulum, monoglucuronide, diglucuronide, canalicular bile)
new_contribution: Hepatocyte processing of bilirubin has four steps: uptake, cytosolic binding, conjugation and secretion. Albumin-bound unconjugated bilirubin is taken up by the hepatocyte (the albumin is not), binds the cytosolic protein ligandin, is conjugated to glucuronic acid in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the mono- and diglucuronides are actively transported into canalicular bile.
reason: Book gives three steps and omits cytosolic binding (ligandin), ER site and active canalicular transport of mono/diglucuronides.

source_excerpt: Conjugated bilirubin is not taken up by the intestinal mucosa. When the conjugated bilirubin reaches the distal ileum and colon, it is hydrolyzed to unconjugated bilirubin.
topic: Intestinal fate of conjugated bilirubin
book_has: p245: 'The gut bacterial deconjugate most bilirubin to colorless urobilinogen'; Fig 35.3 p392 'Bacterial deconjugation'. Site and non-absorption not stated (searched: intestinal mucosa, distal ileum, proximal small bowel, hydrolyzed)
new_contribution: Conjugated bilirubin passes unchanged through the proximal small bowel and is not absorbed by the intestinal mucosa; only in the distal ileum and colon is it hydrolysed to unconjugated bilirubin, which gut bacteria then reduce to colourless urobilinogens.
reason: Adds anatomical site and the non-absorption of conjugated bilirubin, absent from book.

source_excerpt: The remaining 10–20% of the urobilinogens are passively absorbed, enter the portal venous blood, and are re-excreted by the liver.
topic: Fate of reabsorbed urobilinogen (enterohepatic vs urinary)
book_has: p245: '10-20% of urobilinogen are reabsorbed in the ileum and colon and escape enterohepatic circulation and pass to the kidney to be excreted in urine.'
new_contribution: Source: about 80–90% of urobilinogens are excreted in faeces (as stercobilinogen/stercobilin); the 10–20% that are absorbed enter the portal blood and are re-excreted by the liver, and only a small fraction escapes hepatic uptake and is excreted in urine (source figure: ~80% faeces, ~18% enterohepatic, ~2% urine). Book p245 states the absorbed 10–20% escape the enterohepatic circulation and are excreted in urine.
reason: Source and book differ on whether the reabsorbed 10–20% mainly recirculates to the liver or goes to urine. Source's '(usually <3 mg/dL)' urinary figure has doubtful units and is not carried into the contribution.

source_excerpt: About half of the ammonia arising from the intestine is synthesized by bacteria, the remainder coming from dietary protein and glutamine.

new_contribution: Ammonia comes from breakdown of proteins, amino acids, purines and pyrimidines; about half of intestinal ammonia is made by bacteria, the rest from dietary protein and glutamine. The liver normally converts ammonia to urea (urea/ornithine cycle, mainly in the liver and to a lesser extent the kidney) and glutamine. Blood ammonia is elevated in 90% of patients with hepatic encephalopathy, and brain levels are also increased.

source_excerpt: This might be due to increased metabolism by skeletal muscle and kidneys, secondary to the hyperinsulinemia of chronic liver disease.

The imbalance lets more aromatic amino acids cross an abnormal blood–brain barrier; raised brain phenylalanine inhibits dopa production and leads to false neurotransmitters.
